name: Reflection and Evaluator–Optimizer
question: Is this draft good enough, or should it go round again?
summary: A generator drafts, an evaluator critiques the draft against clear criteria, and the generator revises until the draft passes or a round limit is hit. Self-Refine uses one model for every role; Reflexion keeps written lessons from failed attempts for the next try. The gains depend on feedback grounded in something outside the model: tests, rules or a checklist.
useCases: There is a clear standard to check against: tests, a rulebook, a schema
Drafts improve measurably with specific feedback
One or two extra rounds of latency are acceptable

items.detail: one call drafts, another evaluates and gives feedback, in a loop
the same model drafts, critiques and revises
written lessons from failures are stored and reused on the next attempt
tests, validators, rule tables: the most reliable signal
pass, or a round cap; always keep the best draft

steps: Write the evaluation criteria first: tests, rules or a checklist
Turn each failure into a specific written critique
Revise with the critique, then evaluate again
Cap the rounds and return the best-scoring draft, not the last one
pitfalls: Self-critique with no external signal can make answers worse
Unbounded loops burn tokens on marginal gains
Returning the last draft instead of the best one ships regressions
remember: Critique against something real. Keep the best draft.
caption: Illustrative: a draft checked against 10 rules; each critique lists only the rules that failed.

code.text: failed = [l for l in p.stdout.splitlines() if l.startswith("FAILED")]
if best_fails is None or len(failed) < best_fails:
lessons.append(ask("One-line lesson from these failures:\n" + critique))

steps.title: Generate a first draft
steps.text: The model writes an EMI calculator from the spec. Nothing is checked yet, so this is only a candidate.

steps.title: Evaluate against something real
steps.text: pytest runs 10 tests on the draft. 6 pass and 4 fail. The feedback comes from outside the model, which is what makes the loop reliable.

steps.title: Turn failures into a critique
steps.text: The failing test names and messages become a short, specific critique, such as test_zero_rate: ZeroDivisionError, instead of “please improve”.

steps.title: Revise with the critique
steps.text: The model rewrites the code with the critique in view. Version 2 passes 9 of 10, and the loop goes round again.

steps.title: Remember lessons across tasks
steps.text: When a task ends with failures, a one-line lesson is saved and added to the next task's prompt. That is Reflexion's idea: learn from the attempt, not just revise within it.

steps.title: Cap the rounds and keep the best
steps.text: Version 3 passes all 10 tests, so the loop stops at round 3 of 4. Had it hit the cap, it would return the best-scoring version, not the last one.

pros: Large gains when feedback is external: tests, rules, schemas
No training; works with any model
Critiques are readable, so failures are easy to debug
Reflexion lessons carry improvements to later tasks
cons: Each round adds cost and latency
Self-critique without ground truth can make answers worse
Needs clear, checkable criteria written first
Easy to ship a regression by returning the last draft
avoidWhen: There is no reliable way to check a draft (fix the evaluator first)
Latency budgets allow only one pass

playgroundGuide.scenario: A lending team drafts loan-sanction letters that must contain every mandatory disclosure: rate, tenure, EMI, fees, grievance contact and more. A generator drafts and an evaluator scores the letter, then the generator revises. You choose where the feedback comes from, how many rounds are allowed and whether lessons from earlier letters are remembered.
controls: Click No evaluator, Self-critique or Checklist + rules to choose the feedback source.
Drag the slider to set the maximum number of rounds.
Tick memory to start from lessons learnt on earlier letters, or load a scenario.

outputs.name: Score per round
outputs.meaning: Each draft's score out of 100; red means worse than the draft before it.

outputs.name: Returned score
outputs.meaning: The best draft's score, which is what the loop returns.

outputs.name: Rounds · cost per letter
outputs.meaning: Rounds run and total cost: ₹1.50 per draft plus evaluation.

outputs.name: A revision got worse
outputs.meaning: Whether any revision scored lower than the one before it.

presets.name: Self-critique, 3 rounds
presets.expect: Scores 62 → 70 → 74: best 74 at ₹5.70 per letter. The critic cannot see what is missing.

presets.name: Self-critique, 5 rounds
presets.expect: Scores 62 → 70 → 74 → 71 → 66: later revisions regress; the best (74) is returned for ₹9.50.

missions.text: Reach a score of 90 or more within 3 rounds.
missions.hint: Use the checklist and rules as feedback; self-critique never gets there.

missions.text: Produce a regression using self-critique only.
missions.hint: Give self-critique 4 or 5 rounds and watch the later scores fall.

missions.text: Reach 90 or more at the lowest possible cost per letter.
missions.hint: Memory raises the first draft, so rules feedback reaches 90 in round 2. Cap the rounds at 2 so it stops there: ₹3.25.

tools.best: Agents that write verbal lessons after failed attempts and reuse them on the next try.
tools.ex: A coding agent that stores “check the empty-list case” after failing a test and passes on the next attempt.

tools.best: One model drafts, critiques and revises, with no training or extra models.
tools.ex: Rewrite a customer email three times with the model’s own feedback on tone and clarity.

tools.best: Generator and evaluator nodes with a loop edge, round counter and best-draft tracking in state.
tools.ex: An NDA drafting graph that loops until the rulebook node returns no failures or three rounds pass.
pros: Loop limits and state are explicit
Human review can be added at any node
cons: Graph overhead for a short loop

tools.best: Output guardrails and judge agents that can reject a draft and trigger another attempt.
tools.ex: An output guardrail that checks a letter for the grievance contact and fails the run if it is missing.
cons: Guardrails stop runs rather than revise by default

tools.best: Exact, external feedback for generated code: failing test names and messages become the critique.
tools.ex: Loop an EMI calculator until all 10 tests pass, feeding back only the failing lines.
cons: Only as good as the tests
Needs a sandbox to run generated code

goals: Explain why external feedback beats self-critique
Calculate the cost of a revision loop from pass rates per round
Explain why the loop must return the best draft, not the last

practice.scenario: A legal-tech team drafts NDA clauses for Indian and UK clients. Each draft is checked against a jurisdiction rulebook written as code: governing law named, a confidentiality term stated, no non-compete for Indian employees, mutual obligations, and so on. Failed rules become a written critique, the model revises, and the loop stops when every rule passes or after three rounds, returning the best draft seen.

industries.use: Revise contract clauses until they pass a jurisdiction rulebook
Revise loan-sanction letters against mandatory disclosure checklists
Revise generated code until the unit tests pass

practice.analogy: A student and an examiner with a marking scheme. The examiner marks against the scheme and says what is missing; the student rewrites; the best copy is the one handed in.

library.name: Anthropic Python SDK (plain loop)
library.what: Evaluator–optimizer is a short loop: generate, check with code, critique, revise. The checks are ordinary functions or tests.

practice.note: RULES is a list of (name, check function) pairs written by your legal team. Keep the checks in code, not in the prompt.

numericDrill.question: Each generation or revision call costs ₹1.50 and each evaluation by an LLM judge costs ₹0.40; every draft is evaluated. 50% of letters pass on the first draft, 30% after one revision and 20% after two. What is the average cost per letter, in ₹?

interview.question: Why does self-critique sometimes make answers worse?
interview.answer: Without an external signal, the model judges its own work with the same blind spots that produced it, and research found models can change correct answers to wrong ones. Ground the evaluator in tests, rules, a schema or retrieved facts, and keep the best draft rather than the last.

interview.question: How is Reflexion different from Self-Refine?
interview.answer: Self-Refine loops within one attempt: draft, critique, revise. Reflexion works across attempts: after a failed try, the agent writes a short lesson into memory and reads it on the next attempt, which helped most when the feedback came from tests or the environment.

mistakes.mistake: Returning the final draft after the round cap
mistakes.fix: Track the best-scoring draft and return that

mistakes.mistake: Using a vague critique such as “improve this”
mistakes.fix: List the specific checks that failed and why

quiz.question: A coding agent’s generated functions fail tests about 30% of the time. The team has a full unit-test suite. Which loop fits best?
options: Evaluator–optimizer with the test results as feedback
quiz.explanation: Tests are exact external feedback, which is what makes an evaluator–optimizer loop reliable.

quiz.question: Asked to double-check its maths answers with no external tool, a model changes several correct answers to wrong ones. What does research suggest?
options: Without external feedback, models struggle to self-correct and can get worse
Self-critique only fails on long answers
quiz.explanation: Studies found LLMs struggle to self-correct reasoning without external feedback, and performance can drop.

quiz.question: Generation costs ₹1.50 and evaluation ₹0.40, every draft is evaluated, and 50% pass on draft 1, 30% after one revision and 20% after two. What is the average cost per letter?
A clause-revision loop tracks the best draft but ends with return draft. Round 4 scored lower than round 3. What is shipped?
quiz.explanation: Returning the last draft ships the regression. Return the best-scoring draft instead.

quiz.question: Which make a good evaluator for a policy-wording loop? Select all that apply.
options: A rules table checked in code
The generator’s own opinion with no criteria
quiz.explanation: Checkable, external criteria give specific feedback. Vague instructions and unguided self-opinion do not.

quiz.question: What distinguishes Reflexion from Self-Refine?
options: Reflexion stores written lessons from failed attempts and reuses them on later attempts
quiz.explanation: Self-Refine revises within one attempt; Reflexion keeps verbal lessons in memory across attempts.

quiz.question: A product-description loop has no round cap, and some items go through 12 rounds for tiny gains. What is the fix?
options: Cap the rounds and stop when the criteria pass
quiz.explanation: Cap rounds and stop on pass; unbounded loops burn tokens on marginal gains.

quiz.question: Reflexion reported what pass@1 on HumanEval, against 80% for GPT-4 at the time?
quiz.explanation: Reflexion reached 91% pass@1 on HumanEval using test feedback.

quiz.question: A loan-letter loop improves from 62 to 92 in three rounds with rules feedback. Which choices would lower cost without losing quality? Select all that apply.
options: Store lessons from earlier letters so first drafts start higher
Stop as soon as every check passes
quiz.explanation: Memory raises first drafts and early stopping avoids extra rounds. Self-critique lowers quality and removing the cap raises cost.

quiz.question: A critique says “the clause could be clearer”. The revision barely changes. What would help most?
options: A critique that lists the specific failed rules and why
quiz.explanation: Specific failures tell the generator exactly what to fix; vague critique produces vague revisions.

quiz.question: When does Anthropic suggest the evaluator–optimizer workflow fits?
options: When there are clear evaluation criteria and iterative refinement adds measurable value
quiz.explanation: Evaluator–optimizer suits tasks with clear criteria where feedback measurably improves the output.

quiz.question: Self-Refine reported roughly what average improvement across seven tasks, without training?
quiz.explanation: Self-Refine reported about a 20% absolute average improvement across seven tasks.

quiz.question: A dispute-reply loop scores drafts 70, 82, 79, 85 over four rounds. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.
options: The loop should return the round 4 draft, the best
The loop should return the round 3 draft
quiz.explanation: Round 3 fell from 82 to 79, a regression; the best overall is round 4 at 85, which is also the last here.

quiz.question: A grading loop uses an LLM judge that has never been checked against human graders. What is the main risk?
options: The loop optimises towards a miscalibrated judge
quiz.explanation: An uncalibrated judge steers revisions in the wrong direction. Calibrate the evaluator before trusting it.

quiz.question: Each round costs ₹1.60 and memory adds a one-off ₹0.05. With memory, a letter reaches its target in 2 rounds; without, in 3. What is saved per 1,000 letters with memory?
Which task gains least from a reflection loop?
options: Policy letters checked against a rules table
A creative slogan with no agreed criteria
SQL queries checked by running them on a test database
quiz.explanation: With no clear criteria, the evaluator has nothing reliable to check, so revisions add cost without dependable gains.

quiz.question: A reflection loop for SQL generation should include which of these? Select all that apply.
options: Running the query on a test database and returning errors as critique
Raising the temperature on each round
quiz.explanation: Execution feedback, a round cap and best-draft tracking are the core of a safe loop. Raising the temperature adds noise, not feedback.

quiz.question: An NDA loop’s evaluator is a second model call that reviews the draft against a jurisdiction checklist. In Anthropic’s terms, this pattern is:
quiz.explanation: One call generates and another evaluates and gives feedback in a loop: evaluator–optimizer.

quiz.question: A letter passes 6 of 10 checks. Each round fixes 2 of the remaining failures. How many revision rounds until all 10 pass?
quiz.explanation: 4 failures remain; fixing 2 per round needs 2 revision rounds.

quiz.question: Which feedback sources count as external for a discharge-summary loop? Select all that apply.
options: A schema validator for required sections
A check of drug names against a formulary
The same model asked whether it is confident
A second draft by the same model
quiz.explanation: Validators and reference checks are grounded outside the model. Self-reported confidence is not, and a second draft from the same model is not an independent check.
